Q: When do multiple samples, critique loops and decomposition make answers worse?
A: Repeated generation can reinforce a shared mistake because the samples are correlated, not independent sources of truth. A critique model can prefer persuasive wording over correctness, and decomposition can propagate a wrong intermediate assumption through every later step. Use these techniques when a verifiable intermediate contract and budget justify them. Check observable outputs and external evidence rather than treating a longer explanation as proof. Stop when additional rounds no longer improve validated outcomes or exceed the allowed latency and cost.
Why: Five samples can agree on the same outdated policy because all read the same wrong passage. Majority vote does not repair missing evidence; source selection and applicability need correction first.
Risk: Self-agreement can be mistaken for independently verified confidence.
Trade: Additional inference is useful only when measured improvement exceeds its cost and risk.
Try: Construct a shared-evidence error and compare voting with an independent source check.
